newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel urges calm in Lebanon, frees up PLO funds.
newsitem.headline: Israel urges calm in Lebanon, frees up PLO funds.

text.p: Israel strove on Tuesday to defuse tensions in the region, distancing itself from fighting in Lebanon that killed at least nine civilians and promising to transfer Palestinian funds frozen after a suicide attack.
Lebanese militiamen led by pro-Israeli commander Antoine Lahd shelled Lebanon's southern port of Sidon on Monday, killing six civilians and wounding 36, many seriously, security sources said.
Israel strongly denied firing the shells and blamed it on forces serving under Lahd around the Jezzine area outside the occupation zone patrolled by Israel and Lahd's South Lebanon Army (SLA).
"The SLA fire was without the knowledge of the Israeli army," Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said.
"We have no interest in exacerbating the situation or to worsen it, on the contrary, we have an interest in stabilising the situation," he said.

Mordechai said he would urge Lahd not to violate a ceasefire agreement that ended a major Israeli military offensive in April 1996 with an understanding by the parties to the conflict not to target civilians.
It was the first time Sidon had been shelled since Israel launched its offensive.
Shortly after the shelling of Sidon, six Katyusha rockets struck Jezzine, a Lahd stronghold, killing a 60-year-old man, pro-Israeli militia sources said.
Israeli military officials said Lahd's men were apparently avenging the deaths of three youths killed by a roadside bomb in the Jezzine area.
SLA and Red Cross sources said the explosion killed two people.

Israel's chief military spokesman, Oded Ben-Ami, identified two of the youths as the 11-year-old daughter and 17-year-old son of Lahd's late commander in Jezzine, Assad Nasr. Ben-Ami blamed Hizbollah, the pro-Iranian "Party of God", for the attack.
Hizbollah is fighting to drive Israel out of a 15 km (nine mile) deep border zone set up inside Lebanon with the declared aim of preventing guerrilla attacks on Israel's northern border.
The head of Israel's northern command, Amiram Levine, urged Hizbollah not to strike at northern Israel.
"We are doing our utmost not to hit civilians and I hope and advise Hizbollah not to make a mistake and try to hit Israeli civilians," Levine told reporters.
In Jerusalem, Israel was scheduled to transfer on Tuesday to the Palestinian Authority (PA) about a third of the funds it froze after a double suicide bombing in Jerusalem on July 30.
Nabil Abu Rdaineh, an aide to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, welcomed the move calling it a "positive first step".

The United States, which had criticised Israel's freezing of taxes and customs duties owed to the Authority, also hailed the partial thaw saying it brought the resumption of peace talks a step closer.
"We fell a little better today than we did yesterday about the prospect for getting the peace process back on track," State Department spokesman James Rubin said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's spokesman, Shai Bazak, said the decision followed "partial cooperation" by the PA in the investigation into the twin bombing that killed 16 people, including the two bombers.
Israel's Treasury said 42 million shekels ($12 million) would be handed over to the self-rule administration.
After the attack, Israel clamped a security closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip and froze the transfer of funds.
Israel has called on Arafat to launch a major crackdown on suspected militants from the Hamas and Islamic Jihad groups, something the Palestinian president has so far refused to do.
Substantive talks between Israel and the Palestinians have been deadlocked since Israel broke ground in March on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
